title: Homework 1: Benchmarking Methods of Matrix/Vector Multiplication
text: package also contains second function, mult_Ainv_c, multiplies inverse square matrix vector. AA square matrix cc conformable vector, (least) two common ways compute −1cA^{-1}c: Solve linear system Ax=cAx = c directly (direct = TRUE). avoids explicitly forming −1A^{-1}. Compute −1A^{-1} first multiply cc (direct = FALSE). usually slower can less numerically stable. , can use microbenchmarking compare two approaches across matrix dimensions.
code: benchmarks2 <- bench::press(   dims = seq(10, 100, by = 10),   {     A <- matrix(rnorm(dims^2), nrow = dims)     c <- rnorm(dims)     bench::mark(       "solve(A, c)" = mult_Ainv_c(A, c, direct = TRUE),       "solve(A) %*% c" = mult_Ainv_c(A, c, direct = FALSE)     )   } ) #> Running with: #>     dims #>  1    10 #>  2    20 #>  3    30 #>  4    40 #>  5    50 #>  6    60 #>  7    70 #>  8    80 #>  9    90 #> 10   100  benchmarks2 <- benchmarks2[, c("expression", "dims", "median")] colnames(benchmarks2) <- c("Method", "Dimensions", "CPUTime") benchmarks2$Method <- factor(benchmarks2$Method, levels = c("solve(A, c)", "solve(A) %*% c"))  ggplot(data = benchmarks2, aes(x = Dimensions, y = CPUTime, color = Method)) +   geom_point() +   labs(title = "Benchmarking Methods for Computing A^{-1}c",        x = "Matrix/Vector Dimension",        y = "Median Time",        color = "Method") +   bench::scale_y_bench_time(base = NULL) +   theme_bw()

what: Problem 1: Simulate Multivariate Normal Random Vectors (Cholesky)
title: Homework 2: Matrix Decomposition
text: package contains function, rmvnorm, simulates multivariate normal distribution. , informally validate using sample mean/covariances computations. True Sigma Sample Covariance
code: # Simulate 100 realizations of a 4-dimensional multivariate normal distribution set.seed(12345) # Generate a mean vector mu <- rpois(4, 1) # Generate a covariance matrix A <- matrix(rpois(16, 1), nrow = 4) A[upper.tri(A)] <- 0 Sigma <- crossprod(A)  # Simulate from the multivariate normal distribution mvn_sims <- rmvnorm(mean = mu,                     cov = Sigma,                     N = 100)  # Compute the sample mean and compare sample_means <- rowMeans(mvn_sims) compare_means <- data.frame("True" = mu,                             "Sample" = sample_means,                             "Relative Difference" = (mu - sample_means) / mu) kableExtra::kable(compare_means) # Compute sample covariance sample_covs <- cov(t(mvn_sims))  # Create tables kableExtra::kable(Sigma, digits = 3, caption = "True Sigma") |>   kableExtra::kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) kableExtra::kable(sample_covs, digits = 3, caption = "Sample Covariance") |>   kableExtra::kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

what: Problem 2: Evaluate Multivariate Normal Density (Cholesky and Eigen)
title: Homework 2: Matrix Decomposition
text: package contains function, dmvnorm, evaluates density multivariate normal distribution. vignette, run function times different dimensions see runtime scales.
code: # Use bench package for microbenchmarking # bench::press to press results over many dimensions set.seed(12345) benchmarks <- bench::press(   dims = c(4, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256),   {     x <- rep(0, dims)     mu <- rep(0, dims)     A <- matrix(rnorm(dims^2), nrow = dims)     A[upper.tri(A)] <- 0     Sigma <- crossprod(A) + diag(dims) * 0.01      bench::mark(       "Cholesky" = dmvnorm(x, mu, Sigma),       "Eigen" = dmvnorm(x, mu, Sigma, method = "eigen")     )   } ) #> Running with: #>    dims #> 1     4 #> 2    16 #> 3    32 #> 4    64 #> 5   128 #> 6   256  # Plot the results with ggplot library(ggplot2) benchmarks <- benchmarks[, c("dims", "median", "expression")] colnames(benchmarks) <- c("Dimensions", "CPUTime", "Method") benchmarks$Method <- as.character(benchmarks$Method) ggplot(data = benchmarks, aes(x = Dimensions, y = CPUTime, color = Method)) +   geom_point() +   geom_line() +   labs(title = "Benchmarking Multivariate Normal Density Evaluation",        x = "Matrix/Vector Dimension",        y = "Median Time") +   bench::scale_y_bench_time(base = NULL) +   theme_bw()

what: Benchmark the performance of my_lm() using Cholesky, QR, and SVD
title: Homework 2: Matrix Decomposition
text: Recall computational complexities Cholesky, QR, SVD 𝒪(np2+p3)\mathcal{O}(np^2 + p^3), 𝒪(np2)\mathcal{O}(np^2), 𝒪(np2+p3)\mathcal{O}(np^2 + p^3) respectively. , dataset n=300n=300 p=6p=6.
code: benchmarks <- bench::mark(   "Cholesky" = my_lm(y ~ 0 + ., data, "chol"),   "QR" = my_lm(y ~ 0 + ., data, "qr"),   "SVD" = my_lm(y ~ 0 + ., data, "svd"),   iterations = 1000 )  benchmark_times <- do.call(c, benchmarks$time) benchmarks_df <- data.frame(   method = rep(names(benchmarks$expression), each = 1000),   time = benchmark_times ) ggplot(benchmarks_df, aes(x = method, y = time)) +   geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +   labs(title = "Benchmarking Linear Regression Methods",        x = "Method",        y = "Time in Nanoseconds, Log Scale") +   theme_bw() +   scale_y_log10()

title: Homework 4: EM and HMMs
text: consider mixture two normal distributions unknown means μ1,μ2\mu_1, \mu_2 known variances σ1=1.0\sigma_1 = 1.0, σ2=0.8\sigma_2 = 0.8. Pairs (x1,y1),…,(xn,yn)(x_1, y_1), \ldots, (x_n, y_n) ..d. joint distribution Pr(xi,yi)=[αf(yi,μ1,σ1)]𝟏{xi=1}[(1−α)f(yi,μ2,σ2)]𝟏{xi=2}, \Pr(x_i, y_i)  = [\alpha f(y_i, \mu_1, \sigma_1)]^{\mathbf{1}\{x_i = 1\}}   [(1 - \alpha) f(y_i, \mu_2, \sigma_2)]^{\mathbf{1}\{x_i = 2\}}, xi∈{1,2}x_i \\{1,2\} class membership variable indicates distribution gave rise yi∈ℝy_i \\mathbb{R}, Pr(xi=1)=1−Pr(xi=2)=α, \Pr(x_i = 1) = 1 - \Pr(x_i = 2) = \alpha, f(x,μ,σ)=1σ2πexp(−(x−μ)22σ2). f(x, \mu, \sigma)  = \frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}}    \exp\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right). also assume observe y=(y1,…,yn)y = (y_1, \ldots, y_n) observe x=(x1,…,xn)x = (x_1, \ldots, x_n). goal infer α\alpha, μ1\mu_1, μ2\mu_2 maximizing observed data log-likelihood ℓ(α,μ1,μ2)=∑=1nln[αf(yi,μ1,σ1)+(1−α)f(yi,μ2,σ2)]. \ell(\alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) = \sum_{=1}^n    \ln\left[ \alpha f(y_i, \mu_1, \sigma_1)   + (1 - \alpha) f(y_i, \mu_2, \sigma_2) \right]. Instead maximizing log-likelihood directly, want derive EM algorithm get MLEs.

title: Homework 4: EM and HMMs
text: complete-data likelihood, taking product ..d. variables, becomes Pr(x→,y→∣α,μ1,μ2)=∏=1n[αf(yi∣μ1,σ1)]𝟏{xi=1}[(1−α)f(yi∣μ2,σ2)]𝟏{xi=2}. \Pr(\vec x, \vec y \mid \alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) = \prod_{=1}^n \Big[ \alpha f(y_i \mid \mu_1, \sigma_1) \Big]^{\mathbf{1}\{x_i=1\}} \Big[ (1-\alpha) f(y_i \mid \mu_2, \sigma_2) \Big]^{\mathbf{1}\{x_i=2\}}. Taking logs gives lnPr(x→,y→∣α,μ1,μ2)=∑=1n𝟏{xi=1}(lnα+lnf(yi∣μ1,σ1))+𝟏{xi=2}(ln(1−α)+lnf(yi∣μ2,σ2)). \ln\Pr(\vec x, \vec y \mid \alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) = \sum_{=1}^n \mathbf{1}\{x_i=1\} \Big( \ln \alpha + \ln f(y_i \mid \mu_1,\sigma_1) \Big) + \mathbf{1}\{x_i=2\} \Big( \ln (1-\alpha) + \ln f(y_i \mid \mu_2,\sigma_2) \Big). Using lnf(y∣μ,σ)=−ln(σ2π)−(y−μ)22σ2, \ln f(y \mid \mu,\sigma) = -\ln(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}) -\frac{(y-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}, complete log-likelihood becomes lnPr(x→,y→∣α,μ1,μ2)=∑=1n𝟏{xi=1}[lnα−ln(σ12π)−(yi−μ1)22σ12]+∑=1n𝟏{xi=2}[ln(1−α)−ln(σ22π)−(yi−μ2)22σ22]. \begin{aligned} \ln\Pr(\vec x, \vec y \mid \alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) &= \sum_{=1}^n \mathbf{1}\{x_i=1\} \left[ \ln\alpha -\ln(\sigma_1\sqrt{2\pi}) -\frac{(y_i-\mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2} \right] \\ &\quad+ \sum_{=1}^n \mathbf{1}\{x_i=2\} \left[ \ln(1-\alpha) -\ln(\sigma_2\sqrt{2\pi}) -\frac{(y_i-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2} \right]. \end{aligned}

title: Homework 4: EM and HMMs
text: want derive expression 𝔼[lnPr(x→,y→∣α,μ1,μ2)|y→,α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k)]. \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \ln\Pr(\vec x, \vec y \mid \alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) \;\middle|\; \vec y, \alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)} \right]. expectation taken respect conditional distribution Pr(x→∣y→,α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k)). \Pr(\vec x \mid \vec y, \alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)}).  , treat y→\vec y current parameter values α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k)\alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)} fixed, average latent class indicators x→\vec x. complete log-likelihood linear indicator variables 𝟏{xi=1}\mathbf{1}\{x_i = 1\} 𝟏{xi=2}\mathbf{1}\{x_i = 2\}, taking expectations simply replaces indicator conditional probability. Define pi(k)=Pr(xi=1∣yi,α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k)) p_i^{(k)}  = \Pr(x_i = 1 \mid y_i, \alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)}) notational convenience. 𝔼[𝟏{xi=1}∣yi]=pi(k),𝔼[𝟏{xi=2}∣yi]=1−pi(k). \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\{x_i=1\} \mid y_i] = p_i^{(k)},  \qquad \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\{x_i=2\} \mid y_i] = 1 - p_i^{(k)}. Therefore expected complete log-likelihood becomes 𝔼[lnPr(x→,y→∣α,μ1,μ2)∣y→,α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k)]=∑=1npi(k)[lnα−ln(σ12π)−(yi−μ1)22σ12]+∑=1n(1−pi(k))[ln(1−α)−ln(σ22π)−(yi−μ2)22σ22]. \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}\left[\ln\Pr(\vec x, \vec y \mid \alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) \mid \vec y, \alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)}\right] &= \sum_{=1}^n p_i^{(k)} \left[ \ln\alpha -\ln(\sigma_1\sqrt{2\pi}) -\frac{(y_i-\mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2} \right] \\ &\quad+ \sum_{=1}^n (1-p_i^{(k)}) \left[ \ln(1-\alpha) -\ln(\sigma_2\sqrt{2\pi}) -\frac{(y_i-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2} \right]. \end{aligned} important idea randomness complete-data log-likelihood comes unobserved labels xix_i. idea behind EM replace unknown class labels current probabilities, maximize weighted log-likelihood get new parameter estimates, repeat convergence.

title: Homework 4: EM and HMMs
text: maximize, take partial derivatives respect α\alpha, μ1\mu_1, μ2\mu_2. respect α\alpha, ∂∂α𝔼[lnPr(x→,y→∣α,μ1,μ2)∣y→,α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k)]=∑=1npi(k)α−∑=1n1−pi(k)1−α=0. \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \mathbb{E}\left[\ln\Pr(\vec x, \vec y \mid \alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) \mid \vec y, \alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)}\right] = \sum_{=1}^n \frac{p_i^{(k)}}{\alpha} - \sum_{=1}^n \frac{1-p_i^{(k)}}{1-\alpha} = 0. Solving α\alpha, get α(k+1)=∑=1npi(k)n. \alpha^{(k+1)} =  \frac{\sum_{=1}^n p_i^{(k)}}{n}. Checking second derivative, ∂2∂α2=−∑=1npi(k)α2−∑=1n1−pi(k)(1−α)2<0, \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \alpha^2} = -\sum_{=1}^n \frac{p_i^{(k)}}{\alpha^2} - \sum_{=1}^n \frac{1-p_i^{(k)}}{(1-\alpha)^2} < 0,  critical point maximum. respect μ1\mu_1, ∂∂μ1𝔼[lnPr(x→,y→∣α,μ1,μ2)∣y→,α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k)]=−∑=1npi(k)(yi−μ1)σ12=0. \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu_1} \mathbb{E}\left[\ln\Pr(\vec x, \vec y \mid \alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) \mid \vec y, \alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)}\right] = -\sum_{=1}^n p_i^{(k)} \frac{(y_i - \mu_1)}{\sigma_1^2} = 0. Solving μ1\mu_1, get μ1(k+1)=∑=1npi(k)yi∑=1npi(k). \mu_1^{(k+1)} =  \frac{\sum_{=1}^n p_i^{(k)} y_i}{\sum_{=1}^n p_i^{(k)}}. Checking second derivative, ∂2∂μ12=−∑=1npi(k)σ12<0, \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \mu_1^2} = -\sum_{=1}^n \frac{p_i^{(k)}}{\sigma_1^2} < 0,  critical point maximum. respect μ2\mu_2, ∂∂μ2𝔼[lnPr(x→,y→∣α,μ1,μ2)∣y→,α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k)]=−∑=1n(1−pi(k))(yi−μ2)σ22=0. \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu_2} \mathbb{E}\left[\ln\Pr(\vec x, \vec y \mid \alpha, \mu_1, \mu_2) \mid \vec y, \alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)}\right] = -\sum_{=1}^n (1-p_i^{(k)}) \frac{(y_i - \mu_2)}{\sigma_2^2} = 0. Solving μ2\mu_2, get μ2(k+1)=∑=1n(1−pi(k))yi∑=1n(1−pi(k)). \mu_2^{(k+1)} =  \frac{\sum_{=1}^n (1-p_i^{(k)}) y_i}{\sum_{=1}^n (1-p_i^{(k)})}. Checking second derivative, ∂2∂μ22=−∑=1n1−pi(k)σ22<0, \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \mu_2^2} = -\sum_{=1}^n \frac{1-p_i^{(k)}}{\sigma_2^2} <0,  critical point maximum. Therefore, EM algorithm given following updates: pi(k)=Pr(xi=1∣yi,α(k),μ1(k),μ2(k))=α(k)f(yi∣μ1(k),σ1)α(k)f(yi∣μ1(k),σ1)+(1−α(k))f(yi∣μ2(k),σ2),=1,…,n,α(k+1)=∑=1npi(k)n,μ1(k+1)=∑=1npi(k)yi∑=1npi(k),μ2(k+1)=∑=1n(1−pi(k))yi∑=1n(1−pi(k)). \begin{aligned} p_i^{(k)} &= \Pr(x_i = 1 \mid y_i, \alpha^{(k)}, \mu_1^{(k)}, \mu_2^{(k)}) \\ &= \frac{\alpha^{(k)} f(y_i \mid \mu_1^{(k)}, \sigma_1)}{\alpha^{(k)} f(y_i \mid \mu_1^{(k)}, \sigma_1) + (1-\alpha^{(k))} f(y_i \mid \mu_2^{(k)}, \sigma_2)}, \ \qquad = 1, \ldots, n, \\ \alpha^{(k+1)} &= \frac{\sum_{=1}^n p_i^{(k)}}{n}, \\ \mu_1^{(k+1)} &= \frac{\sum_{=1}^n p_i^{(k)} y_i}{\sum_{=1}^n p_i^{(k)}}, \\ \mu_2^{(k+1)} &= \frac{\sum_{=1}^n (1-p_i^{(k)}) y_i}{\sum_{=1}^n (1-p_i^{(k)})}. \end{aligned}

title: Homework 4: EM and HMMs
text: Now, test performance EM algorithm simulating data known mixture normals checking can recover true parameters. Now, plot results : Notice , , initialized EM algorithm 25th 75th percentiles data mu1_init mu2_init, respectively. Let’s see results change opposite:  Now, everything’s reversed! known “label switching” problem likelihood symmetric μ1\mu_1 μ2\mu_2, EM algorithm can converge either mode depending initialization. fix issue, can enforce consistent labeling convention, always labeling component smaller mean component 1. way, always μ1<μ2\mu_1 < \mu_2, algorithm converge mode regardless initialization. Going back original results, question asked bias α̂\hat \alpha associated Monte Carlo error: bias small relative α\alpha, Monte Carlo error larger bias, suggesting estimator unbiased.
code: set.seed(123)  # True parameters alpha_true <- 0.3 mu1_true <- 2.1 mu2_true <- 5.2 sigma1 <- 1 sigma2 <- 0.8 datasets <- 100 n_obs <- 300  results_list <- vector("list", length = datasets) for (d in 1:datasets) {   # Simulate data   x <- rbinom(n_obs, size = 1, prob = 1 - alpha_true) + 1  # x_i = 1 or 2   y <- ifelse(x == 1,               rnorm(n_obs, mean = mu1_true, sd = sigma1),               rnorm(n_obs, mean = mu2_true, sd = sigma2))    # Run EM algorithm on simulated data   rslt_sim <- em_mixture_normals(y,                                  mu1_init = quantile(y, 0.25),                                  mu2_init = quantile(y, 0.75),                                  sigma1 = sigma1, sigma2 = sigma2)    # Store results   results_list[[d]] <- list(     alpha = rslt_sim$alpha,     mu1 = rslt_sim$mu1,     mu2 = rslt_sim$mu2   ) } # Run EM algorithm with reversed initializations results_list_reversed <- vector("list", length = datasets) for (d in 1:datasets) {   # Simulate data   x <- rbinom(n_obs, size = 1, prob = 1 - alpha_true) + 1  # x_i = 1 or 2   y <- ifelse(x == 1,               rnorm(n_obs, mean = mu1_true, sd = sigma1),               rnorm(n_obs, mean = mu2_true, sd = sigma2))   # Run EM algorithm on simulated data with reversed initializations   rslt_sim <- em_mixture_normals(y,                                  mu1_init = quantile(y, 0.75),                                  mu2_init = quantile(y, 0.25),                                  sigma1 = sigma1, sigma2 = sigma2)   # Store results   results_list_reversed[[d]] <- list(     alpha = rslt_sim$alpha,     mu1 = rslt_sim$mu1,     mu2 = rslt_sim$mu2   ) } #> Bias of alpha: 0.002112956 #> Monte Carlo error of alpha: 0.003439607

title: Parameter Estimates for Mixture of Two Normal Distributions via EM Algorithm — em_mixture_normals
text: EM algorithm iteratively performs two steps: E-step: Computes posterior probability (responsibility) observation belongs first component, given current parameter estimates. M-step: Updates mixing proportion component means maximizing expected complete-data log-likelihood. standard deviations (sigma1 sigma2) held fixed throughout algorithm. Convergence assessed based maximum absolute change parameters successive iterations.
